lesson.title: Nationality Adjectives: Spotting the -o/-a and -ense Pattern
lesson.subject: spanish

contentBlocks.text: You already know how to greet someone the right way in Spanish — now it's time to say something about yourself: where you're from. In English, 'American' or 'Peruvian' doesn't change no matter who's talking. In Spanish, a word for nationality actually changes its ending depending on whether it's describing a man or a woman — and once you learn the pattern, you can guess dozens of nationality words you've never even studied.

Your [[la identidad]] is everything that makes you, you — your name, your family, the things you love, and your [[la nacionalidad]], the country you belong to. Spanish has a simple, powerful pattern for talking about nacionalidad: most nationality words end in -o when they describe a man and -a when they describe a woman, exactly like other descriptive words you'll meet later this year. A man from Colombia is [[colombiano]]; a woman from Colombia is colombiana — same word, different ending. A man from Peru is [[peruano]]; a woman from Peru is peruana. Notice the pattern repeats no matter which country you start with — that's what makes it a pattern instead of a fact to memorize one country at a time.

Not every nationality word follows the -o/-a rule, though. Some end in -ense, and those words never change no matter who they describe — a man and a woman from the United States are both [[estadounidense]]. You'll meet other -ense nationalities later on (canadiense, costarricense), and the rule is the same every time: one form fits everyone.

Look at each nationality word below and predict the missing form before checking with your teacher or parent:

- colombiano → colombiana (you already know this pair)
- peruano → ______ (predict the feminine form)
- mexicano → ______ (a brand-new country — does the same -o/-a pattern still work?)
- estadounidense → ______ (predict: does it change for a man vs. a woman?)
- canadiense → ______ (another -ense word — same rule?)

If you predicted peruana, mexicana, and estadounidense/canadiense unchanged, you've cracked the pattern.

Today you learned that most Spanish nationality words change their ending for gender (-o/-a), while a smaller group ending in -ense stays exactly the same either way. Tomorrow you'll use these words as clues in a guess-who game about famous Spanish-speaking celebrities.

objectives: State the general nationality-adjective pattern: -o for masculine, -a for feminine, and -ense as an invariant ending
Produce the correct gendered form of a nationality adjective (colombiano/colombiana, peruano/peruana) given the other form
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Ask the child if any English descriptive words change based on the gender of the person they describe (they don't — 'American' stays 'American' no matter who it describes). This sets up why Spanish is different.
2. Introduce identidad and nacionalidad as the week's big-picture words.
3. Walk through the -o/-a pattern with colombiano/colombiana and peruano/peruana, then the invariant -ense pattern with estadounidense.
4. Work through the pattern-spotting practice list together, having the child predict each missing form before you confirm it.
5. Complete the worksheet.
6. Preview tomorrow's guess-who game with famous Spanish speakers.
differentiationTips: Struggling: start with just one pair (colombiano/colombiana) and confirm the -o/-a swap works before introducing a second country — mastering one full pair beats memorizing four half-understood ones
Ready for more: ask them to guess the feminine form of mexicano or the pattern for canadiense before being told, using only today's rule
If the child asks why estadounidense doesn't have two forms, compare it to English words like 'happy' — some words just don't change, and -ense nationality words are that category in Spanish
teacherGuide.answerKey: 1. peruano → peruana. 2. mexicano → mexicana (the pattern holds even for a country not explicitly taught). 3. estadounidense → estadounidense (no change). 4. canadiense → canadiense (no change, same -ense pattern).
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Opens week 2's WA-WL-2015.1.1 Interpersonal Communication target with the grammatical pattern the scope-and-sequence names as Day 1's specific job (pattern-spotting nationality endings) — teaching it as a rule the student can apply to new words, not a vocabulary list to memorize one country at a time, per the band's emphasis on patterns that unlock many words at once.
